old: Tracking with decision support may reduce deaths in patients with hypertension and diabetes (OR 0.61 [0.35, 1.06]) and new cardiovascular events in high-risk adults (OR 0.58 [0.42, 0.80]), but may make little or no difference to adverse pregnancy outcomes (OR 0.99 [0.87, 1.12]) [1].
new: Tracking with decision support plus targeted client communication (tracking + CDSS + TCC) may reduce deaths in patients with hypertension and diabetes (OR 0.61 [0.35, 1.06]) and new cardiovascular events in high-risk adults (OR 0.58 [0.42, 0.80]), but may make little or no difference to adverse pregnancy outcomes in women receiving antenatal care (OR 0.99 [0.87, 1.12]) [1].

old: The tools probably make little or no difference to the number of women giving birth in a hospital (one study, 799 participants) [2].
new: We are not sure whether the tools change the number of women giving birth in a hospital (one study, 799 participants); the review rates this evidence as moderate certainty in its summary table but low certainty in its detailed table [2].

old: Digital tracking with decision support or reminders probably makes little or no difference to some types of health outcomes, and we are uncertain about others, including maternal and neonatal deaths, because the evidence is very low-certainty [2].
new: Digital clinical decision-support systems accessed by primary healthcare providers on mobile devices probably make little or no difference to some types of health outcomes, and we are uncertain about others, including maternal and neonatal deaths, because the evidence is very low-certainty [2].

old: Tracking combined with messaging or decision support (TCCMD) may increase exclusive breastfeeding among pregnant and postpartum women in settings where it is less common (RR 1.30, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.59; low-certainty evidence), but has little or no effect where almost all women breastfeed (low-certainty evidence) [3].
new: Targeted client communication via mobile devices (TCCMD) may increase exclusive breastfeeding among pregnant and postpartum women in settings where it is less common (RR 1.30, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.59; low-certainty evidence), but has little or no effect where almost all women breastfeed (low-certainty evidence) [3].

old: Tracking combined with decision support or messaging via mobile devices may increase antenatal appointment attendance (OR 1.54, 95% CI 0.80 to 2.96), but this is low-certainty evidence and the confidence interval includes both benefit and harm [3].
new: In pregnant and postpartum women, targeted client communication via mobile devices (versus standard care) may increase antenatal appointment attendance (OR 1.54, 95% CI 0.80 to 2.96), but this is low-certainty evidence and the confidence interval includes both benefit and harm [3].

old: Tracking combined with client communication via mobile devices may reduce any maternal health problem (RR 0.19, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.79) and any newborn health problem (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.25 to 1.06) up to 10 days postpartum, based on low-certainty evidence, though the newborn interval includes both benefit and harm [3].
new: Targeted client communication via mobile devices (TCCMD), compared with non-digital targeted client communication (e.g. pamphlets), may reduce any maternal health problem (RR 0.19, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.79) and any newborn health problem (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.25 to 1.06) reported up to 10 days postpartum, based on low-certainty evidence, though the newborn interval includes both benefit and harm [3].

old: For pregnant and postpartum women living with HIV, mobile-device tracking combined with client communication (TCCMD) may make little or no difference to maternal and infant antiretroviral adherence compared with standard care (low-certainty evidence) [3].
new: For pregnant and postpartum women living with HIV, TCCMD may make little or no difference to maternal and infant adherence to antiretroviral therapy compared with standard care (low-certainty evidence) [3].

old: Based on 10 trials, tracking combined with communication via mobile devices (TCCMD) may modestly increase health service use such as vaccinations and HIV care compared with standard care (RR 1.21, 95% CI 1.08 to 1.34; low-certainty evidence), though effect estimates varied widely between studies [3].
new: Based on 10 trials, TCCMD may modestly increase health service use such as vaccinations and HIV care compared with standard care (RR 1.21, 95% CI 1.08 to 1.34; low-certainty evidence), though effect estimates varied widely between studies [3].

old: Compared with digital non-targeted communication, tracking with targeted communication on mobile devices may reduce vaccination attendance, but the confidence interval includes both benefit and harm (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.33 to 1.20; low-certainty evidence) [3].
new: Compared with digital non-targeted communication, targeted communication via mobile devices (TCCMD) may reduce vaccination attendance, but the confidence interval includes both benefit and harm (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.33 to 1.20; low-certainty evidence) [3].

old: The effect of these digital tracking and messaging approaches on other outcomes is unknown, because too few studies have measured them [3].
new: The effect of targeted client communication via mobile devices on other outcomes is unknown, because of a lack of studies [3].

old: No trials, in any population, reported data on unintended consequences, so possible harms of these mobile tracking and prompt or reminder interventions remain unassessed [3].
new: No trials, in any population, reported data on unintended consequences, so possible harms of these targeted communication (TCCMD) interventions remain unassessed [3].

old: The effect of these interventions on health service use is unknown because there is a lack of studies [3].
new: For pregnant and postpartum women, the effect of these interventions on health service use compared with non-digital communication (e.g. pamphlets) is unknown because there is a lack of studies [3].

old: For use of health services, effects on skilled attendance at birth are uncertain (very low-certainty evidence), and the intervention may make little or no difference to antenatal influenza vaccination attendance (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.58; low-certainty evidence), though the CI includes both benefit and harm [3].
new: For TCCMD versus digital non-targeted communication, effects on skilled attendance at birth are uncertain (very low-certainty evidence), and the intervention may make little or no difference to antenatal influenza vaccination attendance (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.58; low-certainty evidence), though the CI includes both benefit and harm [3].

old: In a review of text reminders for HIV care, some trials excluded people who were illiterate or had no phone, and the authors judged it likely that most trials excluded people without a personal mobile phone [4].
new: In a review of mobile phone messaging trials, two trials of text reminders for HIV antiretroviral care (in Mozambique and Brazil) excluded people who were illiterate, had no phone, or both; because only one trial stated that it provided phones, the authors judged it likely that all other trials excluded people without a personal mobile phone [4].

old: Tracking combined with targeted client communication on mobile devices may modestly increase contraception use (RR 1.19, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.35), based on low-certainty evidence [4].
new: Targeted client communication via mobile devices may modestly increase contraception use among adolescents compared with standard care (RR 1.19, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.35), based on low-certainty evidence [4].

old: The effects of these tracking-plus-prompt or reminder interventions on abortion rates and on antiretroviral therapy (ART) adherence are unknown, because no studies were found [4].
new: For targeted client communication via mobile devices (TCCMD) compared with digital non-targeted communication, the effects on abortion rates and on antiretroviral therapy (ART) adherence are unknown because of a lack of studies for this comparison [4].
